questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the doctrinal basis for challenging an unclear term
questions.stem: Clause 1 of the memo says the zoning overlay permits structures that are of reasonable proportion to the adjacent lots. Which reason best supports challenging that term?

options.text: A law must give ordinary people a fair chance of knowing what it forbids
The overlay covers too much land, so it reaches a large amount of protected activity
options.misconception: confuses the vagueness doctrine with overbreadth

options.text: The overlay lacks a sufficient procedure for hearings before denial
options.misconception: misidentifies procedural sufficiency as clarity

options.text: The overlay permits too many uses near residential districts
options.misconception: treats a planning judgment as a constitutional defect

questions.explanation: A law is vague when ordinary people cannot know what it forbids or when it invites arbitrary enforcement. Overbreadth and procedure are separate doctrines that this wording does not trigger.
questions.hint: Focus on what the words tell a person to do.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret data on a compelled affirmation requirement
questions.stem: Clause 2 of the memo records permit applicants who were asked to sign a statement endorsing a city ordinance, with eighteen applicants refusing. Which inference does the data support?

options.text: Most applicants supported the ordinance, which shows the statement tracked real belief
options.misconception: infers belief from the rate of signing

options.text: The refusals show the statement was narrowly drafted and easy to understand
options.misconception: draws a clarity conclusion from refusal counts

options.text: Refusing to affirm the ordinance did not block any permit, so the compulsion was avoidable
Eighteen refusals prove the requirement is too vague to enforce consistently
options.misconception: mistakes disagreement for vagueness

questions.explanation: A compelled affirmation is unconstitutional where a person can decline, and the permits issued despite refusals. Clarity does not save it, since the issue is the forced utterance.
questions.hint: Ask whether the affirmation could be declined.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how symbolic expression is analyzed
questions.stem: Clause 4 of the memo asks how the city should treat flags flown outside the planning office. Explain how symbolic expression is analyzed under First Amendment principles.

answer.exemplar: A flag is not protected merely because it is a symbol, because it also communicates and can be used to harass or intimidate. A flag display on government property may be regulated for reasons of order and message neutrality, and a school or public employee may face different rules than a private citizen displaying the same symbol.

questions.explanation: Symbolic expression is analyzed for its message and context, and protected only so far as it communicates. A flag in a school or workplace is judged differently from one in a private display.
questions.hint: Consider both the message conveyed and the setting.

questions.explanation: Compelled disclosure is judged on the degree of intrusion and on whether a protective option exists. The clause offers a declination line and keeps the list confidential, favoring the city.

Only the first, because a fixed number always constrains design choices

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the framework for student expression
questions.stem: Clause 13 of the memo describes a rule limiting student distribution of leaflets. Explain the framework a court uses to decide whether the rule is valid.

answer.exemplar: A court asks whether the student expression is substantially disruptive of the school educational mission or materially infringes on the rights of others. If the disruption is substantial, the school may restrict the expression; if the disruption is minor, the school may impose reasonable time, place, and manner limits but may not ban the speech itself.

questions.explanation: Student expression is protected unless it is substantially disruptive or infringes others rights. Even then the response must be reasonable in scope, and a total ban on leafleting usually fails.
questions.hint: Focus on disruption and the reasonableness of the response.

questions.learningObjective: Compare two standards under the vagueness doctrine
questions.stem: Clause 17 of the memo compares two permit standards: structures that do not obstruct sight lines and structures of a moderate scale. Which comparison best applies the vagueness doctrine?

options.misconception: believes referring to an object resolves vagueness

options.misconception: assumes deference cures unclear standards

options.misconception: condemns all standards involving evaluation

questions.explanation: Vagueness asks whether a standard gives fair notice, and a moderate scale standard may be upheld if practice supplies meaning. A sight line standard without guidance leaves officials free to act arbitrarily.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the standard for compelled affiliation
questions.stem: Clause 31 of the memo discusses a rule requiring permit applicants to disclose every organization they support. Explain the governing standard for such a rule.

answer.exemplar: A court weighs the intrusion the requirement creates against the government interest in enforcing the permitting rules, and the requirement is constitutional only if it is narrowly drawn to serve that interest. questions.explanation: Compelled association is a serious intrusion, so the requirement must be narrowly tailored to the interest asserted and supported by findings. The rule asking about every organization strains that fit.
questions.hint: Weigh the intrusion against the interest asserted.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the vagueness test
questions.stem: Clause 40 of the memo asks how a court decides that a term is too vague to enforce. Explain the test a court applies.

answer.exemplar: The court asks whether the ordinary person, guided by the most common understanding of the term and the text and context of the statute, can know what conduct is prohibited or what conduct is required. It also asks whether the term invites arbitrary or discriminatory enforcement by those charged with applying it, and a term that fails either inquiry cannot survive.

questions.explanation: A vagueness challenge succeeds when ordinary people cannot know what the law requires or when it invites arbitrary enforcement. The rule fails only if the text and context fail both inquiries.
questions.hint: Test the term against what ordinary people can understand.

questions.explanation: Requiring a plain statement of standards, listed factors, and written appeals reduces the chance a vague rule is enforced arbitrarily, and gives a court something to review. It is a safeguard rather than a source of rights.
questions.hint: Note what the safeguard asks the agency to publish.
